name: message
intent: Package the information a boundary must carry into one self-describing unit - a header section the messaging infrastructure can read, route and mediate on, plus a body that travels unchanged - so that senders, mediators and receivers share a uniform unit of communication without sharing a payload schema.
problem: A boundary must carry data between parties that do not share a domain model. Without one agreed unit of communication every endpoint invents its own record shape: the transport cannot route, filter, enrich, trace or selectively log without parsing payloads, each mediator becomes coupled to every payload schema, and adding a consumer, a transport or a policy means renegotiating the framing with every producer.
context: Message-oriented and request/response boundaries between processes, services or systems - brokers and queues, RPC, HTTP, mail, event buses - where more than two parties (or middleware the endpoints do not own) inspect the traffic, where the payload format must evolve independently of routing metadata, and where the transport should stay replaceable. The decision is a data-shape one, taken together with the channel (Message Channel) and the message type (Command/Document/Event Message).
benefits: One uniform unit for all infrastructure: channels, routers, filters, enrichers, wire taps and tracers read, rewrite and dispatch on header metadata without parsing or understanding the payload.
Payload independence: the body's format and schema evolve on their own schedule, because the messaging system's contract is only the header vocabulary.
Extensibility by design: new metadata (correlation, trace context, content type, expiry, history) arrives as headers, so neither the transport nor the payload schema has to change.
Transport portability: the same message maps onto different transports - broker, HTTP, mail, queue - by binding header fields to the transport's native metadata instead of re-encoding the body.
Uniform policy and observability at the boundary: authentication, authorization, throttling, dead-lettering, auditing and tracing can be applied to headers for all messages alike.
Cheap routing: content-based routing and filtering become header lookups rather than body parsing, which keeps brokers and gateways stateless and fast.
tradeoffs: Two contracts to evolve: the header schema and the body schema drift apart, and moving a field between the two sections breaks every mediator that reads the old location.
Header names and value types are a public interface: renaming or retyping a header is a breaking change for routing rules and policies that the producer does not own.
Self-description invites over-description: header bags grow into untyped, undocumented optional fields nobody dares to remove, with no compile-time safety in dynamic languages.

Security exposure: metadata is attacker-controlled unless the channel authenticates the message, so routing, identity and correlation headers are spoofable and header injection (into logs, SQL, templates) is a real vulnerability class.
Overhead: metadata is duplicated and re-encoded at every hop, header size and count limits are small, and large payloads force an out-of-band reference (Claim Check) instead of a message.
Opaque bodies raise debuggability and governance cost: brokers and monitoring see metadata only, so understanding traffic needs endpoint tooling and disciplined content types.
Smuggling: producers hide routing-relevant data in the body so mediators must parse it after all, silently re-coupling the parts the pattern separated.

participants.responsibility: The atomic package: exactly one header section and one body, travelling together over a channel and delivered as a whole (no half-messages).

Metadata section written by senders and mediators - origin, destination, type, correlation id, timestamp, expiry, content type, trace context - that the messaging system reads to route, filter and enforce policy.
The payload section carrying the domain data; opaque to the messaging system and transported unchanged, interpreted only by endpoints that understand its content type.
The transport between endpoints that keeps the header/body package intact and may inspect or add headers; it moves the message and never interprets the body.
Assembles the message: fills both sections, sets routing, correlation and lifetime metadata, and hands the whole package to a channel.
Decides from the headers whether and how to process the message, interprets the body with the schema its content type names, and may add or consume metadata (acknowledgement, redelivery flags).
Router, translator, enricher, filter or wire tap: reads and rewrites headers without touching the body, and adds its own metadata (history, trace, transformation provenance).

use_cases: Events and commands across services on a broker, where record/message headers carry the routing and idempotency metadata and the key/value or body carries the payload.
HTTP and gRPC APIs: request and response types pair a header block with a content-typed body, and gateways, sidecars and proxies route on the metadata alone.
Integration middleware that must route, filter, enrich or translate traffic for schemas it does not own — the mediators work entirely in the header section.
Store-and-forward packages such as mail (MIME headers plus body) and file transfer, where disposition, content type and origin live in headers and the payload stays opaque.
Long-running asynchronous workflows: correlation id, causation id, trace context, timestamp and expiry ride in the headers while payloads stay domain-specific and versioned independently.
Dead-lettering and message store scenarios where a message must be captured, inspected and replayed later; the header/body split makes both metadata queries and payload replay possible.

Kafka and event-streaming platforms: messages carry partition keys, offset metadata, schema version and trace context in headers while the body carries the domain event, enabling platform tooling to operate without payload parsing.

Cross-bounded-context integration with DDD: each bounded context owns its payload semantics; the envelope carries only technical metadata (type, version, source, tenant) so an anti-corruption layer can translate at context boundaries.
CDC (Change Data Capture) feeds from databases, where the envelope carries operation type, change sequence, source system and capture timestamp while the body carries the changed record.

Multi-region and multi-tenant platforms: envelope metadata carries tenant markers, region indicators and security classifications so routing, isolation and compliance auditing operate at the infrastructure layer.

Spring Integration's Message<T> abstraction: MessageHeaders carries correlation, content type and routing metadata while getPayload() remains the application payload, letting channels and endpoints mediate without owning its schema.

RabbitMQ AMQP publishers: Basic properties and headers (content type, message ID, correlation ID, reply-to, expiration and delivery mode) travel separately from the message body, so exchanges and consumers can use delivery metadata while payload codecs remain endpoint-owned.

Apache Camel routes: org.apache.camel.Message keeps a body, headers, message ID and timestamp inside an Exchange, so processors can enrich or route metadata while leaving payload handling to endpoints.
avoid_when: The call is in-process and synchronous: a method call with typed parameters - or a single Parameter/Context Object when the argument list is long - is simpler and faster than a message package.
One closed system with one protocol and one schema consumes the data: a serialized Data Transfer Object over that protocol already is the unit of communication, and a header bag adds only ceremony.
The payload is bulk or streaming data: chunk the stream or use Claim Check instead of wrapping a huge body in one message with metadata.

Routing information would be the domain data itself: if mediators genuinely need fields from the payload, model those fields explicitly (Property-Based Serializer) rather than pretending the body is opaque.
anti_patterns: Stringly-typed header bag: dozens of optional, undocumented, untyped headers that only one service reads, forming a second schema nobody versions.
Business logic in headers: routing or policy decisions on mutable application state (status, price, stock) so that mediators silently become part of the domain logic.
Serializing live domain objects or native serialization into the body, so the message can only be read by one runtime and one class version.
Envelope re-invention per endpoint pair: every producer/consumer pair defines its own framing, so no router, tracer or dead-letter queue can treat traffic uniformly.
Trusting unauthenticated headers: acting on caller-supplied routing, return-address, identity or correlation metadata without authenticating the message.
Naked payload: putting only business fields in the body and relying on broker-specific tribal knowledge for everything else — works until versioning, replay or multi-team governance is needed.

Payload swamp: stuffing domain data, transport metadata, retry counters, topic names, technical flags and routing hints into the body, making the event a serialised pile of anxiety instead of a business fact.
Conflating occurredAt and publishedAt: using a single timestamp for both the business fact and the transport event, which breaks reconciliation when consumers lag or retries happen.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: infrastructure metadata (headers) versus domain data (body).
Information hiding: the body is opaque to the messaging system, so mediators cannot depend on payload schemas.
Stable published contract: header names, value types and the content type are a public interface, versioned like any other API.
Layer discipline: nothing above the boundary needs to see the wire envelope, and nothing below it needs to decode the payload.
Single responsibility per section: routing metadata in headers, business data in the body, nothing duplicated between the two.
best_practices: Keep the body opaque to infrastructure; if a mediator must read a field, promote it to a header (or move the mediator outside the boundary).
Freeze and document header names, types and value ranges, version the message contract, and tolerate unknown headers (Tolerant Reader) so producers can extend safely.
Authenticate or sign the message before trusting routing, identity, return-address or correlation headers, and treat header values as untrusted input.

Prefer standard envelopes — CloudEvents context attributes, JMS headers, AMQP properties, HTTP header fields — over a custom header vocabulary so third-party tooling can route and observe the traffic.
Bound metadata: enforce header-size and count limits, and hand large payloads to Claim Check instead of stuffing them into the header section.
Put lifetime, correlation and trace metadata in the headers (Message Expiration, Correlation Identifier, Return Address) and never duplicate it in the body.
Distinguish business time (occurredAt) from integration time (publishedAt, processedAt) — store both in the envelope, as conflating them is a common source of reconciliation bugs.
Use message decorators to attach system metadata (trace context, request IDs, partition keys) transparently at the transport boundary rather than polluting the domain payload.
Apply the transactional outbox pattern: generate envelope metadata (messageId, occurredAt, aggregateId) close to the originating transaction so provenance is never reconstructed from logs.
Version event semantics deliberately: if meaning changes materially, publish a new event type rather than bumping a version number silently — version numbers are cheap, semantic discipline is not.
For multi-language estates, prefer schema-first formats (Protobuf, Avro with Schema Registry) over JSON for envelope bodies to get compile-time safety and cross-language code generation.
Duplicate critical routing and correlation metadata in both broker headers and envelope body during migration phases — this enables replay tooling to work without broker-specific replay.
Treat the envelope as a stable published interface: even inside one organisation, an undocumented header field is a breaking change that the producer does not own.
sources: Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns: Designing, Building, and Deploying Messaging Solutions (2003) — Message pattern (Chapter 3, Messaging Systems).
